item.title: Why We Delay Important Decisions
item.description:
Decision-Making

Why We Delay Important Decisions

Understanding what drives delay can make big decisions easier to face.

Posted November 2, 2026

Key points
  • People often delay decisions because uncertainty makes them uncomfortable.
  • Avoidance of a decision brings temporary relief but prolongs stress.
  • Overcoming procrastination requires aiming for a "good enough" outcome and starting with a small step.
Source: Aron Visuals / Unsplash

I’m sure you can relate to putting off an important decision until next week, then the week after that, and then the week after that. Maybe you need to decide where you would like to relocate, choose a healthcare provider, or determine whether to move forward with an important medical procedure. You know the decision needs your attention, but you keep finding reasons to wait.

Most of us may think of procrastination as putting things off because we are busy or lack motivation. However, what if we are not avoiding the task itself, but the uncertainty that comes with making a decision? Oftentimes, the most difficult part is not knowing what to do, but accepting that we cannot predict how things will turn out.

Escaping Discomfort

Experts argue that one reason this happens is negative reinforcement. When avoiding something uncomfortable brings relief, our brains will likely desire to avoid it again. Consider, for example, when a deadline gets pushed back. In the moment, you may feel better knowing you have more time to complete the task at hand, even though you know that the work still needs to get done. Delaying an important decision can have the same effect. We may receive temporary relief, however the decision still remains unresolved.

In my work with people facing difficult life decisions, I have seen how the desire to avoid making the wrong choice can become a significant barrier. People may spend considerable time weighing possibilities, seeking reassurance, and revisiting the same concerns.

Why We Keep Looking for the Best Choice

Another reason important decisions can be difficult to make is that we want to make the best possible choice. Experts describe this tendency as maximizing. It involves searching for the best available option, rather than choosing one that meets our needs and priorities. Wanting to make a good decision is reasonable, but constantly searching for something better can make it harder to settle on an option.

Let's think about someone deciding whether to relocate for a new job. The opportunity they are considering may offer better pay and career growth, however accepting it could mean leaving family, familiar surroundings, and comfort. They may continue comparing options and questioning whether another opportunity would have been better, even after obtaining enough information to inform their decision.

Recent research offers some insight into this pattern. For instance, in a 2024 study, researchers examined how people with maximizing tendencies estimate the time they spend making decisions. Results showed that "maximizers" tended to underestimate how much time they spent comparing and reconsidering their options. They likely don't realize they are making decision-making harder not easier for themselves.

When More Choices Make It Harder to Decide

Making a decision becomes even more challenging when we are faced with too many options to select from. For instance, someone who has decided to undergo a medical procedure, but must choose how to pay for it, has to decide on using a credit card, applying for a medical credit line, choosing an in-house payment plan, or financing through a third-party company, which adds another decision to an already important one.

One emerging example in the healthcare industry is "first-look financing." An article by Cherry describes how this concept introduces one preferred financing option first while keeping other options available. This approach reflects choice architecture, which examines how the presentation of choices can influence people's decisions.

For example, after a patient agrees to move forward with a medical procedure, the clinic might first explain its preferred third-party financing option, including the monthly payment and application process. If the patient is not comfortable with that option, the provider can then discuss other options, such as an in-house payment plan or using a credit card.

Practical Steps to Move Forward

Here are a few ways to make important decisions feel more manageable:

  1. Start with one small step. When a decision feels overwhelming, try to avoid focusing on everything that needs to happen at once. Identify one manageable action, such as making a phone call, gathering information from a trusted friend, or scheduling an appointment. Taking that first step can make the larger decision feel less difficult.
  2. Narrow your options. You do not need to explore every possibility available. Instead, try to focus on two or three realistic choices and identify what matters most to you at that moment. Setting a reasonable boundary on how much time you spend researching can help prevent you from repeatedly comparing the same options.
  3. Aim for a "good-enough" decision. We often want to feel certain that we are making the right choice. However, waiting for an option with no disadvantages can keep us from moving forward. Look for a choice that meets your needs and makes sense for your current situation. You can only make the best decision possible with the information you have at the time.
  4. Recognize when you are avoiding the decision. Ask yourself whether you genuinely need more information or whether you are putting off the decision because you feel uncomfortable with the uncertainty. A question to ask could be: "Am I waiting because I need more information, or because I'm concerned that I will make the wrong decision?"

The Bottom Line

Putting off important decisions is something many of us experience, especially when we are uncertain about what may happen next. Avoiding a decision can make us feel better temporarily, but it does not necessarily make the situation easier. Ultimately, we do not have to find the perfect option or know exactly how everything will turn out before moving forward. Sometimes, making a good-enough decision and taking one small step at a time is what can help us move past the uncertainty.

item.title: A Famous Case of Shared Eyewitness 'Memory'
item.description:
Forensic Psychology

A Famous Case of Shared Eyewitness 'Memory'

A 1914 rumor shows how shared stories can be mistaken for evidence.

Posted November 2, 2026

Key points
  • Eyewitness memory is frequently poor, but it can become disastrous when people share fallacious accounts.
  • Poor memory plus fallacious accounts can contribute to strong, coherent beliefs in things that never happened.
  • In 1914, rumors of nonexistent Russian troops spread widely and were linked to real wartime events.
Source: Matthew Sharps

In previous posts of the Forensic View, we have seen that eyewitness memory, while frequently convincing to jurors and the public, is frequently and sometimes fabulously unreliable. But what happens when our confidence in reported eyewitness information is essentially “wired in parallel,” shared among different people who may, with repetition, put their own stamps on the information?

In 1914, during the First World War, these processes resulted in strongly held beliefs that Russian troops were coming.

To Scotland.

All histories of that terrible conflict discuss the importance of Russian military operations in Eastern Europe. The hardships and horrifying casualty counts of that very harsh campaign are well attested.

But none of that happened in Scotland, where tens of thousands of entirely imaginary Russians were firmly believed to have turned up anyway.

How a Railway Delay Sparked the Russian Troop Rumor in 1914

The whole mess seems to have started on August 27th, 1914, when there was a long delay in the railway service linking London and Liverpool. Somebody, perhaps in an ill-advised attempt to boost morale, explained to somebody else that this was due to the diversion of trains which were transporting thousands of Russian troops, who had landed in Scotland, to reinforce the Western Front.

Word spread. These Russians’ route was allegedly very specific; they had crossed the Arctic Sea to Norway, then traveled by steamship to Aberdeen, and from there were being carried by special troop trains to the Channel ports.

Why Specific Details Make False Eyewitness Accounts Seem Credible

Now, prior frameworks for understanding strongly influence our ability to remember and interpret information (Bransford & Johnson, 1973), even when those frameworks are completely incorrect, and the resulting memories and interpretations are therefore complete rubbish (Sharps, 2024; Sharps & Price-Sharps, 2026). However, when such frameworks, accurate or not, are filled with plausible feature-intensive detail, people may be increasingly inclined to believe them (Sharps, 2022, 2024); and the specificity of these peripatetic Russians’ itineraries helped to convince people of their absolute reality.

Additional details followed. Witnesses had supposedly seen Russians stamping snow off their boots at railway stations (Pennell, 2015). Makes sense—Russia has a lot of snow. Granted, how those troops managed to maintain that snow on their boots all the way to Edinburgh in August is quite a mystery (Tuchman, 1962); but since the story included the very specific detail of an imaginary railway porter who had swept up the imaginary snow, who was going to argue with this imaginary account?

Wartime Stress Helped People Overlook Flaws in the Rumor

Very reliable people had supposedly seen these Russians. An Oxford professor knew a colleague who’d been summoned as a Russian translator, and a Scots army officer had seen their big fur caps and, believe it or not, their bows and arrows. Why these Russian troops lacked modern weapons remains unexplained, but with enough popular momentum behind the story, people believed it anyway. The people of the time were under the extraordinary stress of horrible new types of warfare that produced casualty rates virtually beyond comprehension for that day—and it has been shown that when people are under stress, they are more likely to ignore evidentiary flaws in accounts (Sharps et al., 2013; Sharps, 2024).

Evidently, this psychological effect extended to snow in August and 20th-century Russian infantrymen armed like Robin Hood.

Imaginary Troop Numbers and Real Events Fueled the Rumor

A Scots landowner personally reported 125,000 Russians marching across his property (Tuchman, 1962), which seems a bit low when 500,000 imaginary Russians were originally reported; but gradually these imaginary numbers dropped down to an equally imaginary 70,000 or 80,000, which presumably made people feel more confident about the realism of the whole imaginary business.

Some actual history became involved in this mess, as well. The naval battle of Heligoland Bight, which had nothing whatsoever to do with Russians, was explained as some form of weird diversion to cover the sea transport of these imaginary forces to Belgium (Tuchman, 1962). On the continent, people waited en masse in Paris to welcome their Cossack defenders. The Germans became concerned as well (Tuchman, 1962). Contemporary reports held that the Kaiser and his senior staff had left France from fear of the “250,000” Russian troops believed to be in the field there, and the German Army was reported to have detached two sorely needed divisions to repel this imaginary invasion from the Steppes.

Why the Psychology Behind the 1914 Rumor Still Matters Today

Readers today may find this account mildly amusing, but essentially irrelevant to our modern lives. The First World War seems lost in remote antiquity, with the Red Baron, perhaps better known today for pizza than for aerial victories, flying about in a powered box-kite, and antique cannons being dragged around mud-soaked battlefields by teams of panicked horses. The whole thing may seem as remote to modern people as Crecy or Agincourt.

But if you were able to examine the brain of a person in 1914, you would find no substantive difference between that brain and the one in the head of any modern Internet-ridden person today. The effects of inaccurate prior frameworks, of stress-related reduction in critical thinking, and of the uncritical sharing of purported eyewitness accounts would be psychologically the same in the worlds of 1914 and 2026.

However, there would be an important exception today, based on our technology rather than our psychology. Unlike the word-of-mouth campaigns that spread false rumors in clubs and at railway stations in 1914, we of 2026 have the internet to spread false rumors worldwide at electronic speeds, either by mistake or by design on the part of people who have something to gain. We also have AI-generated imagery so advanced that its products are virtually impossible for most of us to tell from reality.

The remote and imaginary reports of Russians in Scotland in 1914 are more than a quaint episode in the history of eyewitness memory. They form a significant warning for those of us in the modern age of technology. Today, more than in any previous era, we must be very careful in our assessment of evidence, eyewitness, visual, and otherwise, and very aware of how the principles governing our psychology may influence that assessment.

item.title: Have You Ever Had Sex That Felt Scary?
item.description:
Sex

Have You Ever Had Sex That Felt Scary?

Many young adults have, especially women and sexual and gender minorities.

Posted November 2, 2026

Key points
  • In a survey of 721 Indiana University undergraduates, 31% reported at least one scary sexual experience.
  • Women made up 75% of those reporting scary sex; sexual and gender minorities were also vulnerable.
  • Scary experiences included coercion, unwanted roughness, intoxication, restraint, and condom removal.

In 2014, the White House Task Force to Protect Students from Sexual Assault found that 20 percent of college women get raped as undergraduates. The report generated controversy. That many? Really? The controversy spurred research. Three years later, a large study by investigators at many U.S. colleges and universities concluded the statistic was “reasonably accurate.” (Muehlenhard, 2017)

During the decade since that Task Force, many colleges, universities, and the military have instituted rape-prevention programs that inform young women of their risk, warn against getting drunk at parties, and encourage “designated sober” bystanders to intervene if they see trouble. Those programs have reduced women’s risk of sexual assault in higher education and the military by 50 percent.

Rape-prevention programs have also spotlighted the fact that some problematic young-adult sexual interactions don’t constitute sexual assault, but are still unwanted and scary. Recently, Indiana University researchers investigated who experiences scary sex and why.

The Study

The researchers surveyed 721 undergraduates, average age 19, at Indiana University, 49 percent women, 49 percent men, 2 percent other, divided roughly evenly among first-, second-, third-, and fourth-year students. Almost 80 percent were heterosexual, with 12 percent bisexual, 5 percent lesbian/gay, and 4 percent transgender or gender non-binary. Half were single, half in relationships. Completing the 20-minute survey entered them in a lottery for $100 gift cards. (Herbenick, 2025)

One-Third Reported Scary Sex

Almost one-third of survey respondents (31 percent) reported at least one sexual experience they called scary. Three-quarters of them (75 percent) were women, 21 percent were men, and 5 percent were transgender or gender non-binary.

The researchers grouped scary experiences into seven categories:

  • Wouldn’t stop. This was the most reported experience. “When I told him it really hurt and please stop, he didn’t.” “I kept saying stop, but he ignored me.” “Everything was fine until I wanted to stop, but he didn’t.”
  • No control. This was the #2 response. “I felt like I didn’t have a say.” “I was with someone much older than me, and he controlled things.” “I tried to say no, but couldn’t get the words out.” “I felt that if I insisted on stopping, my partner wouldn’t want to date me anymore.”
  • Pressure, coercion, manipulation. “In his room, he pressured me to have sex. I didn’t know what I was walking into.” “I knew him for years and trusted him. Then he pressured me to give him head.”
  • Unwanted roughness. “When things got too rough, I was too scared to say anything.” “I got choked way too hard. I felt overpowered and scared.”
  • Drunk, drugged, unconscious. Alcohol greatly increases sexual assault risk, or short of rape, sex that’s scary. “We were drinking a lot. I don’t remember having sex. That scared me.” “I wanted to leave, but was too drunk to move.” “I was drunk. He was not. He pressured me for sex.” “I was drunk and could not fight back.”
  • Restrained. “He pinned my arms over my head. When I said it hurt, he said I was ruining the mood.” “He held me down. When I objected, he wouldn’t let go.”
  • Condom-related. “He took the condom off without telling me.” “He pressured me to have unprotected sex. That scared me.” “I knew she was inconsistent about taking her pills. She pressured me for intercourse, but I had no protection. That incident ended our relationship.”

This is not the only study to delve into frightening sex. Two pilot reports by Indiana University researchers showed that 25 percent of women and 10 percent of men reported sometimes feeling scared during sex. (Herbenick, 2019, 2022) Those studies inspired this larger one.

Scary sex may include activities that are standard elements of bondage-discipline-sado-masochism (BDSM): restraint, rough play, and sacrifice of control. But in mutually pleasurable BDSM, the players negotiate their play beforehand. They agree to every move, and everyone knows exactly how the play will unfold. They also adopt “safe words” to stop the action if anyone feels uncomfortable or scared.

Young Men, Alcohol, and Sexual Violence

Across all categories, some participants of every gender and sexual preference reported feeling scared. But overwhelmingly, they were women and sexual and gender minorities—and their fear was inspired by male partners. In other words, the problem is out-of-control young men. Parents, older siblings, college staff, and mental health professionals should tell young men repeatedly and bluntly that they better control themselves or they risk prison.

What makes men lose control? Usually alcohol. Although today’s young adults drink less than previous generations, alcohol continues to fuel reckless behavior. Anyone who deals with young people should tell them repeatedly and bluntly that alcohol intoxication may embroil them in situations they would rather avoid. Beer commercials say “drink responsibly.” To prevent scary sex, a better message would be “just one drink if any, no more.”

Young adults experiment with both sex and drugs. We’ve all been there and know that some of those experiments play with fire. To avoid getting burned, young adults should take responsibility for their safety by:

  • Not getting drunk, especially at parties, particularly fraternity parties
  • Not getting sexually involved with those who are drunk
  • Arranging with friends before parties to keep an eye on each other and intervene if things seem to be getting out of hand

Some might call this victim-blaming. It’s not. It’s taking adult responsibility for personal safety. That’s prudent—and as this study shows, unfortunately necessary.

item.title: How to Meditate to Help Reduce Shame
item.description:
Shame

How to Meditate to Help Reduce Shame

A practical guide to interrupting sexual shame spirals with meditation.

Posted November 2, 2026

Key points
  • Meditation creates space between thoughts and your response, making automatic spirals less inevitable.
  • Suffering comes from judgments about a fetish, not the fetish itself.
  • Notice your thoughts without suppressing them or adding commentary, then gently return to your breath.

Meditation is a tool for creating distance between yourself and the onslaught of default thoughts, emotions, and sensations that make up our moment-to-moment experiences. This distance enables choice and provides the most profound type of personal freedom on offer: the freedom to decide how you feel about things, your sexuality being chief among them.

Here is the most basic meditation I’m aware of. Try it if you dare:

  1. Sit down somewhere comfortable. It can be in a chair (like the Germans do), on your couch (like Americans), or cross-legged on the ground (like the Buddha).
  2. Start breathing in through your nose and out through your mouth. Don’t worry about pacing—just breathe to stay alive, per usual.
  3. Notice your breath—like really notice it. Notice the slight coolness inside your nose when you breathe in, the mild but still somehow sharp pressure in your lungs as they fill with air, the subtle tingle on the inside of your lips as air exits through your mouth.
  4. Keep noticing the sensations that arise with your breath. There are a lot of them; they never stop, and they’re always different.
  5. Your mind will wander. Thoughts will pop into your head—thoughts as quotidian as "Jeez, I still need to pack lunch for tomorrow" and as profound as "Man, do I hate Jim." When that happens, simply notice that you are focusing on something other than your breath and bring your attention back to the explosion of stimulation that is your breathing.
  6. Be warned: You will have amazingly urgent thoughts when you’re meditating. Yesterday the cure for cancer popped into my head, and then I realized the perfect thing to say to save my marriage. Each time, I gently noticed that my attention was on something other than my breath, and I brought it back.

You don’t need to spend a ton of time practicing to reap significant benefits. I recommend starting with ten to fifteen minutes a day, three days a week. But even as little as a couple of minutes a week can make a difference.

The benefits of meditation have become so sensationalized by the self-help industry that it’s important to be clear about what its actual purpose is. Meditation will not produce startling insights into the mysteries of the universe. Your IQ and personality will remain unchanged. If you suck at pickleball before meditating, you will suck afterward. But do it enough—starting with a few minutes a few times a week—and you will notice that your mind has become a little less frantic, a little less hooked by doom loops, and a little more spacious.

Meditation is a way to create space between us and our unproductive thoughts, and it can therefore offer relief from shame. Try doing a meditation practice when you feel yourself getting into a negative mindset. When you experience that stench of shame associated with your fetish, notice it as a thought arising out of nowhere. You did not ask for that feeling of shame, and it in no way helps you. Let it go and bring your attention to your breath. It will probably arise again—notice that, and again gently but firmly return your attention to your breath. There is no need for you to react to or add commentary to your shame—don’t pile new thoughts onto the shame thought and don’t recoil from it—just notice it and bring your attention back to the breath.

This is not about avoiding unpleasant thoughts; it is simply about recognizing and not elaborating on them. Shame is just a thought arising in your mind like any other thought, and it is in its nature to pass away (thanks, Buddha). Simply processing your shame thoughts in this way will eventually strip them of their emotional power. So much of our suffering is the result of obsessive elaboration on the things that pop into our heads. Somatic exercises are meant to help us stop piling on.

Allow me to introduce an analogy based on my beloved New York City, whose sidewalks burst with every type of human imaginable, all of whom jump into your field of vision all the time. You can’t control who walks by or what might be on the sidewalk. They simply appear. You might notice the pretty girl, the cold-eyed businessman, the kindly older man helping his wife across the street, or the guy you think is waiting to pick your pocket. Your thoughts are the same. Simply notice them when they pop up next to you on the sidewalk.

Let’s walk through a common shame spiral I see in my work: Imagine you’re scrolling Instagram on the couch. Someone has posted a fashion photo of a person wearing latex. There’s a brief moment of excitement, followed immediately by, "This is so shallow. Why can’t I be turned on by something normal?" That thought brings in the others: "This is weird. I shouldn’t be turned on by this. How can I possibly live a normal life with this desire?" Now your attention is no longer on the image itself—it’s on the story you’re telling about your desire.

From there, the thoughts intensify. You start replaying past rejections—that time you brought a date to the sex toy store, and they judged you for wanting them to try on latex, etc. Within seconds, a neutral moment of arousal has turned into a full-on spiral.

Notice what’s happening here. The fetish didn’t create the suffering. The thought about the fetish did. This is where the sidewalk metaphor becomes useful. You didn’t choose who walked by, but you stopped, stared, followed, and built based on what you saw. A meditation-trained mind might instead note, "Arousal happened," or "That person looks hot in latex," just as it might note, "That smells bad," and then keep moving. The practice isn’t to pretend the sidewalk is empty. It’s to stop writing poems about the pile of sh*t.

Excerpted from my book, Fetish: Smash Taboos and Celebrate What Turns You On.

item.title: Using AI to Avoid Thinking Harms Students
item.description:
Artificial Intelligence

Using AI to Avoid Thinking Harms Students

AI can be helpful when it prompts students to think more.

Posted November 2, 2026

Key points
  • AI can be helpful by testing students regarding their understanding of course material.
  • Learning may be impaired when use of AI eliminates the need to wrestle with an academic topic.
  • Use of AI can lead to missed learning opportunities.
Source: Chayanuphol/Shutterstock

The conclusion of this blog post is so important for students that I want to start with it:

If you are learning something that makes you think, using AI to avoid thinking is a misuse. AI use is appropriate when it prompts you to think more or to help you accomplish “busy work,” which requires little thinking.

In light of this statement, helpful uses of AI in education include:

  • Having an AI test students regarding their understanding of course material, which they might upload into an AI. This could include the “busy work” of preparing flash cards for use in studying the material.
  • An AI giving additional practice problems when students do not answer questions correctly.
  • Asking students to explain concepts they have learned to an AI, and only allowing AI feedback once students have provided their full explanation.
  • Performing literature searches, while ensuring that students verify information provided by an AI through review of primary sources.
  • Providing feedback regarding completed essay drafts or solved problems uploaded by students (but not rewriting the material or solving the problems).
  • Adapting the content and pacing presented educational content based on students’ level of knowledge and ability (Kestin et al., 2025).

Students may suffer when their use of AI reduces or eliminates their need to wrestle with a problem. This impairs learning, because:

  • They will fail to master the required subject matter. Effective education occurs when students struggle with a concept as part of the learning process (Dunlosky et al., 2013).
  • They will be unable to easily use that subject matter as a basis for future learning and understanding. For instance, their future creativity and innovation may be hampered because of an inability to access a broad base of knowledge and understanding in their minds.
  • Their developing brains may not learn how to think about the educational material, and this may weaken development of skills to integrate and elaborate upon difficult information.

I asked seven consecutive adolescent patients who have come to my counseling practice how they have been using AI to help with their schoolwork. Unfortunately, I believe each one of them reported a potentially harmful misuse, which they did not even realize.

As we review these misuses, it should be kept in mind that major goals of education should not be attaining good grades or correct answers, but rather acquiring knowledge and how to better understand and generalize it.

Summarizing Notes

A high school sophomore was given an assignment to take notes about his history reading, and then to summarize what he learned in three sentences. He dutifully read the material and typed his notes into an AI Chatbot. He then asked AI to summarize the notes in three sentences, which he turned in.

Missed Learning Opportunity: Taking notes is an insufficient tool for learning (especially when the notes are typed rather than handwritten). Rather, deciding which is the most salient information from the notes to put into a summary is the activity that best promotes learning from this assignment.

Solving Math Problems

A high school senior was dealing with a difficult homework problem in her math class. She asked an AI to show her how to solve the problem. The AI showed her the step-by-step solution. After she felt she understood the explanation, she went on to study her other subjects.

Missed Learning Opportunity: Just because this student understood the AI-generated explanation did not mean that she could utilize this explanation in solving further problems. She should have worked through a few other similar problems without help of the AI to ensure that she understood how to apply the underlying principles (Bastani et al., 2025).

Summarizing Reading Material

Another high school senior who was taking several advanced placement classes used AI to summarize the highlights of books he was supposed to read for English class. He then wrote essays for this class using the AI-generated material.

Missed Learning Opportunity: How to extract essential information from reading material is a learned skill. While it is tempting to use AI for this purpose, a human reader may find different salient information by reading an original source. For instance, an AI summary may fail to comment regarding how an author presented detailed subject matter intended to evoke a reader’s emotions.

Writing an E-mail

A high school junior asked AI to compose e-mails to his teachers about missed assignments and potential make-up work.

Missed Learning Opportunity: Students should learn how adding a human element as part of a written communication is more likely to generate favorable response. For instance, I quickly delete emailed queries from students requesting the opportunity to work with me if they appear to be AI-generated.

Verifying the News

A high school sophomore told me he has used AI to verify the news he has heard on social media.

Missed Learning Opportunity: Given generative AI’s propensities to hallucinate and echo what it has been told (sycophancy) using AI to verify the news is a poor practice (Fletcher & Verckist, 2025). Instead, this student should learn how to use primary sources to verify news, such as consulting reports by a few news organizations.

The last two examples of potential misuse were prompted by teachers rather than the students:

Making a Poster

An 8th grader was told by his science teacher to use AI to make a poster that presents what he had learned about a particular topic.

Missed Learning Opportunity: While I appreciate the teacher’s desire to teach students how to apply AI in their lives, in 8th grade it might be much more important for students to learn how to apply the elements that make for an effective poster presentation. For instance, how to decide on an appropriate title, choose the effective top line summaries, and what information should be included while maintaining readability of the poster. As part of this process, students also would learn how to prioritize the information they gathered.

Exact Definitions

A 9th grader was given an assignment by his English teacher to define different words, identify their part of speech, and to provide their language of origin. The student completed the assignment without consulting AI, and was downgraded because he didn’t give the exact definition of the word as listed by an AI. Furthermore, the student was aware that his teacher used an AI to grade the assignment.

Missed Learning Opportunity: According to the student in this example, his teacher is enthusiastic about using AI, and teaching students how to do so. Unfortunately, his teacher’s whole-hearted adoption of AI is pushing the student to forego his independent thinking and learning process in favor of allowing AI to shape his work.

Takeaway

Students may be tempted to use AI as a short-cut to complete their assigned work. However, as demonstrated in this blog, learning can be greatly diminished by using AI.

Students’ use of AI to prompt their thinking is good. Their use of AI to avoid thinking is detrimental. Thus, when students face difficulty in understanding an assignment, they should ask for hints from their instructors or an AI, rather than answers.

item.title: Probing the Depths of a Drive-by
item.description:
Personal Perspectives

Probing the Depths of a Drive-by

Personal Perspective: We need imagination to walk in knowledge.

Posted November 2, 2026

Key points
  • “Drive-by” sympathy offers caring words but little effort to understand another’s suffering.
  • Psychic numbing can make caring people less responsive as the scale of suffering grows.
  • Recognizing one's own emotional detachment matters as much as criticizing others’ shallow support.

"Imagination is more important than knowledge"—Albert Einstein

Imagination has an assortment of meanings and often works in different and perplexing ways.

Merriam-Webster defines imagination as “the act or power of forming a mental image of something not present to the senses or never before wholly perceived in reality."

So imagine the term “drive-by.” It has an assortment of definitions. One of the more established is an assault where a perpetrator fires a weapon from a moving vehicle, then flees the scene.

“Drive-by” is also the name of a celebrated rock band—the Drive-By Truckers.

And there are others.

But the most relevant connotation to me, sadly, is when one pretends to care about a person in need or a highly emotive issue, then quickly moves on for various reasons. Among them: Perhaps they simply don’t understand or are overwhelmed by the circumstances; they can’t embrace emotional trauma or disease; or they’re shallow individuals caught up with self-aggrandizement; or they flat-out don’t really care about the health or well-being of others.

Words like callous and self-centered come to mind.

So, they often punt, in words that have no inner meaning.

I find this true in my journey with Alzheimer’s and an advancing prostate and chest cancer diagnosis—diseases embedded in my family. I’m one of millions.

The gut response often tends to be: “But you look so good!”

The truth here is that Alzheimer’s and cancer don’t affect, at the start, how one looks. It’s the inner core of the diseases that torments. And so, in their great uneasiness about discussing the specifics, many punt.

I’ve pondered this over time, working hard not to feel irritated about it. Seems to me, there’s a proclivity these days for many to be absorbed with self. We see it in advertising; we see it in movies; we see it in social conversations about the size of one’s home, investments, money in the bank, or worldly accomplishments and possessions.

With such individuals, a common response to those in need is to espouse in a drive-by at best: “I’m here for you!”

Well, what the heck does that mean? Unless one embraces the need or at least wants to be educated about it, the response comes across as shallow as low tide on Cape Cod Bay, which runs out to the horizon for miles,

Writes Archie James: “The people who don’t really care about you are so difficult to identify. They are present. They are warm enough. They are soft enough on the surface. They say the right words. They are not cold. They say anything like: ‘That’s amazing' and 'I’m so proud of you!’

“On the surface,” adds James, “if you would describe this conversation to someone else, it might sound like support. It would pass the test. But something doesn’t land. You hang up the phone—or leave the room—and you feel vaguely emptier than you did before.”

Many say the perception today that people in general have become more superficial is driven perhaps by advancing technologies, shifts in culture, addiction to social media, or simply checking out from the whirlwind of modern life. We collectively absorb a 24/7 news cycle of wars, world crises, staggering suffering, and crushing violence. And so many of us suffer at times from compassion fatigue, and race to hit the pause button—a numbing defense mechanism worldwide.

Pump the brakes on this. I now realize that I’m in the driver’s seat at times as well—neglecting the needs of others. Research is enlightening.

Commenting on a worldwide scale, Paul Slovic, an academic expert in human judgment, says that many people are generally caring “and will exert great effort to rescue individual victims whose needy plight comes to their attention. These same good people, however, often become numbly indifferent to the plight of individuals who are one of many in a much greater problem.”

It’s called “Psychic Numbing.”

Says the Arithmetic of Compassion: “Psychic numbing is a psychological phenomenon that causes us to feel indifferent to the suffering of large numbers of people. The quote attributed to Joseph Stalin—‘One death is a tragedy; a million deaths is a statistic’—is an illustration of psychic numbing.”

Notes Bessel van der Kolk, a Dutch American psychiatrist and researcher, in his book, The Body Keeps the Score: “Traumatized people (worldwide) chronically feel unsafe inside their bodies. The past is alive in the form of gnawing interior discomfort. Their bodies are constantly bombarded by visceral warning signs, and, in an attempt to control these processes, they often become expert at ignoring their gut feelings and at numbing awareness of what is played out inside. They learn to hide from themselves.”

Author Jessica Sorrensen had it right when she reflected, “I just let the pain take over, allowing it to numb the pain of being left behind.”

And observed Bethany Griffin, author of Masque of the Red Death, “I’ve perfected the art of the fake smile. It’s not so difficult when you are completely numb.”

The fake smile… mea culpa... We’ve all used it.

And so, many caring individuals have become somewhat detached these days, and in many ways for understandable reasons.

So, how do we know what others really feel deep inside? That’s often a crapshoot in these days of political correctness, keeping to party lines, not baring the soul in reflective ways.

How do we rise above this fray?

Perhaps with oxygen tanks. Perhaps not, for now.

Thus, one needs to use imagination to climb out of a box that people place you in when they say they want to help; they want to sympathize, but they don’t.

Fully noted: As an Irish Catholic, I’m thinking now that I need to be back in the confessional on this.

One often needs imagination, I’ve learned the hard way, to walk in knowledge—for knowledge is limited and imagination is vast, as Einstein notes.

Even more so on the lip of holiday times.

item.title: Parental Alienation: Recognizing the Signs Early
item.description:
Parental Alienation

Parental Alienation: Recognizing the Signs Early

A fictional scenario illustrates how parental alienation happens.

Posted November 2, 2026

Key points
  • Parental alienation often starts with a co-parent who is emotionally immature.
  • Because of its insidious nature, knowing how parental alienation hooks a child is critical.
  • Trying to expose a co-parent's manipulation may deepen parental alienation if the child sees it as an attack.

You never thought it could happen to you. Divorce is difficult, but losing the bond with your children is excruciating. You may be the emotionally available parent who has done the bulk of the "real" parenting since your children were born, and your bond has always been strong. Yet, your kids are suddenly cold and rude to you. They avoid being around you and refuse to tell you anything about their life. When you ask if your co-parent is behind their treatment, they become irate and refuse to even speak to you. It is soul-crushing.

Although there can be many reasons for a child's withdrawal from a parent during a divorce, there is a certain type of co-parent who intentionally undermines the opposite parent's relationship with the children. Often, it starts with a co-parent who is emotionally immature and cannot lose face. They strive, always, to protect their ego. Their image means everything to them, so after a divorce, they must come out on top. In addition, this parent, who may lack emotional availability, is often exceedingly jealous of the parent who is emotionally available and who has an authentically close bond with the kids—so they seek to sabotage it. Parental alienation is insidious. So, understanding how it works is critical when attempting to salvage your relationship with your kids.

How Alienation Happens

Picture yourself on the back of a boat in the ocean with your child and co-parent. Your child holds the only life preserver. You and your co-parent are thrown out of the boat in different directions. Thrashing in the water, your co-parent begins to wail to the child, “I am not going to make it! I’m not going to make it! Help me!” Although you are also struggling, you tell your child, “Stay in the boat, honey! Don’t let go of that life preserver. Stay where you are.” But your child is completely panicked by your co-parent's screams, so they jump in the water to try to help them.

As your child and co-parent climb back into the boat, your co-parent says to your child, “I would not have made it without you. I would not be here without you. What would I ever do without you?”

In this scenario, a couple of things are happening. First, your co-parent is playing the victim, and by doing so, sends your child into an intense panic. Kids are psychologically, neurologically, genetically, physiologically, and emotionally programmed to protect their attachment relationship, so when an attachment figure says they do not know if they are going to make it, the child instinctively dives in to help them. The child may ignore their own health, well-being, and emotional needs to take care of their parent, so they do not lose this parent. Second, when the co-parent and child get back to safer ground, the co-parent says something that makes the child believe that they are the only one who can help this co-parent in difficult times, just like they did. That they are this parent’s “lifeline,” so to speak.

Alternatively, you strive to be your child’s protector, not the other way around. You can take care of your own emotional needs and would never burden your child with them. This may be additional evidence that you are an emotionally healthy parent.

Consequences for the Alienated Child

When your child is alienated, they lose their innocence and ability to be a kid because they are consumed with worry about the parent who acts as if they will not survive the “mistreatment” that you are inflicting. This child is burdened by the responsibility of holding your co-parent up. And guess what? Your co-parent exploits this. When the child is disloyal to you, the co-parent acts as if their mental health is repaired, and everything is right in the world. The child feels unburdened from worry for a moment. Naturally, the child then looks for more opportunities to display and discuss their rejection of you so they can continue to relieve themselves of the anxiety that comes from feeling responsible for a parent’s well-being. Your co-parent rewards the child and continues to inappropriately confide in the child about how “unfair” and “devious” you are, improperly sharing adult information.

You are locked out of their life, and it may be the worst pain that you have ever felt. Yet, the more you try to get your child to see the manipulation, the more your child sees you as the “bully” that the co-parent has mischaracterized you as. You feel helpless and hopeless.

You collect data about your co-parent’s emotional mistreatment and negligence, yet every time you bring something up in court, your co-parent denies it and accuses you of worse. The battles in court last for months and years with no real progress. So, what can you do?

Demonstrating Emotional Availability to Your Child

One option is to let your attorney work from the outside in, while you work from the inside out. Focus on rehabilitating your bond, not stopping your co-parent. As an emotionally available parent, you may have important parenting skills that your co-parent seems to lack. You can empathize instead of sympathizing. You can understand a different perspective and honor it. Flexibility comes easy to you, and so does constructively working out conflict. And, most importantly, you can follow through with a boundary or limit in a calm and loving manner.

Additionally, if you are the emotionally invested parent, you may remember the endearing, hilarious, and adorable moments when your child did something incredibly special at a very young age. Your co-parent may not. Patiently waiting for a natural moment to retell a story about your child saving a baby bird when he was 3 or standing up to the neighborhood bully to protect her younger sibling are ways to prove to your child that you have always been there for them and that you have always seen them.

Seize every moment to do the emotionally intelligent things that your co-parent usually cannot do, and never point them out. Allow the child to feel the emotional safety that you provide when they are with you. They may be able to begin to discern how different they feel when they are with your co-parent. Most importantly, never ever give up. You can find more information on this topic in my book, How to Outsmart a Narcissist: Use Emotional Intelligence to Regain Control, at Home, at Work, and In Life.
